chapter_theme: Paripadal 5, to Sevvel: the vel's deeds, the velan's rite placed within the god's bound, the birth from Siva's seed through the sacrificial fire and the six sages' wives, the gifts of the gods, and a prayer for grace, love and aram instead of wealth.

paripadal:5:1-21.reading: The poet hails the spear that went into the wide cold sea until its floor was churned to dust, that rode the tall mount, cut down Sur at the root of his mango form and wiped out the deceiving asuras, and that split the great hill named after the crane; he names the god six-headed, twelve-shouldered, sun-coloured, born in the lotus, red Vel, son of the god of the kaaya tree, and then says that the praise and the possession rite the velan performs at festivals are neither true nor false, since this world has its limit in him and the high and low among all others are in his power.
paripadal:5:1-21.nuance: Lines 16 and 17 are a small theology of the veri rite: the velan's cry is not dismissed as error (as the akam friend dismisses it) nor taken as plain truth; it is valid only because everything stands within the god's bound. Line 10 ends on மூ-இரு கயந்தலை and line 11 opens on the same words, a deliberate linking repetition. சிறப்போய் சிறப்பு இன்றிப் பெயர்குவை (line 18) can be read as 'you who are excellence go about without needing honour'; the sense is not secure. The hill split for its crane name is the one later poets call Krauncha.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his deeds and names: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:5:22-47.reading: The poet tells the birth: the green-eyed brahmin who ate the gods' share of the sacrifice, who with the first brahmin as charioteer, the Veda yoked to the earth for chariot, the serpent for bowstring and the mountain for bow, burned the three forts with one fiery arrow, joined Uma in a marriage whose union would not end; Indra won from the unwinking forehead eye a boon to stop it, and the truthful god, unwilling to take back his gift, split the embryo with a blazing axe; the seven sages, knowing, would not let their wives carry it and poured it as oblation into the fire, and of the seven women who live in the north six ate what remained of the three fires, all but Saalini, the one star, so that the great sages' wives of spotless chastity conceived you without failing in their chastity.
paripadal:5:22-47.nuance: The story is built to keep chastity whole: the mothers conceive through the fire's leftover, not through a man, and the one wife who does not eat (Saalini, the star by the Seven) is singled out. Lines 36 to 41 are compressed and the exact order of the sages' decision (cut, refuse, pour into fire) is a reading, not a certainty.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's birth told as praise, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the bowstring of the archer of the three forts

paripadal:5:48-70.reading: They say the six bore you on a bed of lotus in the green pool of the towering Himalaya; on the day of your birth Indra came with his fire-spitting thunderbolt and struck, and you, cut into six, became six and were one; when in your play-war Indra was left empty-handed, Agni drew from his own body the cock, the rich lord of the sky the peacock with its spotted plumes, and Yama the ram, and with these and the weapons the others gave, bow, sword, spear, axe, pick, the sun, garland and bell, held in twelve hands, you passed beyond the fame of Indra himself.
paripadal:5:48-70.nuance: அறு வேறு துணியும் அறுவர் ஆகி, ஒருவனை (lines 53, 54): Indra's blow, meant to destroy, is what makes him six and one; the gods' gifts come out of their own bodies (தன் மெய்யின் பிரித்து, three times), so the vahanas are presented as parts of the older gods given up to the younger. Lines 65 to 67 (மரனும், கனலியும்) and 70 (கொட்டை) are uncertain in what they name.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's birth, victory and weapons, under paadaan

paripadal:5:71-82.reading: Only those who take up your virtues and hold to aram, the good who bow to great ascetics, reach your shade; those whose hearts burn with lasting anger, those without aram, those whose penance has broken down and the fools who say there is no rebirth do not; so what we ask is not wealth, gold or pleasure but from you grace, love and aram, these three, you who wear the garland of round-clustered kadamba.
paripadal:5:71-82.nuance: The prayer names what it refuses (பொருளும் பொன்னும் போகமும்) before what it asks, and the three it asks are ethical states, not gifts. Among those shut out are மறு பிறப்பு இல் எனும் மடவோர், the deniers of rebirth: a Sangam devotional poem already treats rebirth as a belief whose denial excludes one from the god.

thinai_evidence.note: a prayer to the god: paadaan

links.note: Paripadal 5.1-4 (பனிக் கடல் ... புக்கு ... சூர் மா முதல் தடிந்து) and Thirumurugatruppadai 45-46 and 60 (பனிக்கடல் கலங்கவுள் புக்குச் சூர்முதல் தடிந்த ... மாமுதல் தடிந்த) tell the Sur deed in nearly the same words.
links.teaches: The near-identical phrasing in two different collections shows the Sur killing already had a fixed verbal formula, a shared stock of Murugan praise that both poets drew on rather than one poem borrowing a picture from the other.

links.note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
links.teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

links.note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
links.teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

links.note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
links.teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 151-154 shows Siva only as one of three lords who come to see Murugan, with Uma, three unwinking eyes and the three forts destroyed; Paripadal 5.22-47 tells how that same god's union with Uma led to Murugan's birth.
links.teaches: The guide poem gives the kinship only as epithets (son of the god of the banyan, line 256) and shows Siva as a visiting lord, while the Paripadal narrates the birth in full, so the pair shows the story was known to both but told only where a poem chose to narrate rather than to direct a pilgrim.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 253-255 (நெடும்பெருஞ் சிமையத்து நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை ... அறுவர் பயந்த) and Paripadal 5.48-49 (இமயத்து நீலப் பைஞ் சுனைப் பயந்தோர்) set the birth in the same blue pool and give him six mothers.
links.teaches: Both poems use நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை and the six who bore him, but only the Paripadal says who the six were and why their chastity stayed whole, so the guide poem's single epithet is seen to presuppose a full birth story its hearers already knew.

links.note: Paripadal 5 has six of the seven sages' wives bear him; Thiruppugazh 372 names him the six-faced one who drank at the breasts of the six (அறுவர் முலையுணு).
links.teaches: In the Paripadal the six are mothers by conception through the fire, while in the Thiruppugazh they have become nurses he drank from, so the pair shows the six mothers' role shifting from bearing to nursing as the Krittika story settled.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai ends with the god giving the suppliant a rare gift (பெறலரும் பரிசில்) that makes him stand alone in the world; Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram.
links.teaches: The guide poem frames devotion in the bard's economy of gifts, while the Paripadal explicitly refuses material gifts, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to what one should ask of Murugan, the patron's reward and the ethical state.

links.note: Kural 241 ranks the wealth of அருள் above the wealth of goods, which even the base possess; Paripadal 5.80-81 refuses பொருளும் பொன்னும் and asks அருளும் அன்பும் அறனும்.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the ranking a general maxim about kinds of wealth, and the Paripadal turns that same ranking into the content of a prayer, showing the ethical scale used as the measure of what to ask a god for.

links.note: Paripadal 5 asks Murugan for love (அன்பும்) instead of wealth; Thiruppugazh 986 asks for love growing ever greater, with tears, melting and faltering speech, and only then for the stainless meaning.
links.teaches: The Sangam prayer names love as one of three ethical gifts, while the Thiruppugazh makes love itself the whole request and describes its bodily signs, so the pair traces anbu changing from a virtue asked for into the felt experience of bhakti.

new_concepts.gloss: the velan's rite of possession by Murugu, and the ground where it is performed
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word (Paripadal 5, line 15: வேலன் ஏத்தும் வெறியும்)

source_issues: Paripadal 5: the core text has 82 lines but the source numbers its last line 81 (printed 81 stands on line 82).
Paripadal 5 lines 12-14 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; line 78 differs strongly from theirs; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 5 lines 5, 28 and 70: lost vowel sign ொ restored in the -ஒடு fault (flags).
Paripadal 5 line 31: விண்னோர் is a misprint for விண்ணோர்.
Paripadal 5: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், which is a musical mode, not a thinai.
